title: Human Body
blurb: How your heart, brain, gut, immune system and senses work.

cards.title: A double pump
cards.text: The heart is two pumps side by side. The right side sends blood to the lungs to pick up oxygen; the left side pumps it around the whole body.

cards.title: The circuit
cards.text: Blood makes a figure of eight: body → right heart → lungs → left heart → body. One full lap takes under a minute at rest.

cards.title: A lifetime of beats
cards.text: At around 70 beats per minute, the heart beats about 100,000 times a day and some 2.5–3 billion times in a lifetime.

cards.title: Arteries, veins, capillaries
cards.text: Arteries carry blood away from the heart under high pressure. Veins bring it back, with valves to stop it flowing backwards. Tiny capillaries in between swap oxygen and waste with cells.

cards.title: What's in blood
cards.text: Blood is a little over half plasma (water, salts, proteins) and the rest mostly red blood cells, with white cells and platelets.

cards.title: Red blood cells
cards.text: Red cells carry oxygen using haemoglobin, an iron-rich protein that makes blood red. They have no nucleus, live about 120 days, and you make about 2 million every second.

cards.title: Blood pressure
cards.text: Blood pressure has two numbers: systolic (as the heart squeezes) and diastolic (as it relaxes). A typical healthy reading is around 120/80 mmHg.

cards.title: Blood types
cards.text: Your blood type, A, B, AB or O, depends on markers on red cells; Rh positive or negative adds another. O negative can be given to almost anyone in an emergency.

cards.title: The heartbeat's spark
cards.text: Each beat starts in the sinoatrial node, the heart's natural pacemaker, which sends an electrical pulse across the heart. An ECG records that electricity.

cards.title: Take your pulse
cards.text: Press two fingers on the inside of your wrist below the thumb. Count beats for 15 seconds and multiply by 4. Resting rates of 60–100 are typical for adults.

quiz.q: Where does the right side of the heart pump blood?
What makes blood red?
Which vessels have valves to stop backflow?
quiz.explain: Blood in veins is under low pressure.

lessons.title: The brain and nerves
lessons.summary: 86 billion neurons and how they talk.

cards.title: Neurons
cards.text: The brain has about 86 billion nerve cells. Each neuron receives signals through branches called dendrites and sends them along a long axon to other neurons.

cards.title: Electric and chemical
cards.text: Inside a neuron, signals travel as electrical pulses, up to about 120 m/s. Between neurons, at the synapse, they cross as chemicals called neurotransmitters.

cards.title: Brain regions
cards.text: The cerebrum handles thinking, senses and movement; the cerebellum coordinates balance; the brainstem runs breathing and heartbeat automatically.

cards.title: Four lobes
cards.text: The cerebrum's cortex has four lobes on each side, each with main jobs, though most tasks use many areas working together.

cards.title: Left and right

items.r: Both halves work together in everyone

cards.text: Each half of the brain controls the opposite side of the body. The idea of "left-brained logical" and "right-brained creative" people is a myth; both halves work together.

cards.title: The 10% myth

items.w: We only use 10% of our brain
items.r: We use virtually all of it

cards.text: We don't use only 10% of our brain. Scans show activity all over the brain across a day, and damage to almost any area causes problems.

cards.title: Energy hungry
cards.text: The brain is about 2% of body weight but uses roughly 20% of the body's energy, mostly to keep neurons ready to fire.

cards.title: Reflexes
cards.text: Touch a hot pan and your hand pulls back before you feel pain. Reflexes travel through the spinal cord without waiting for the brain, saving precious milliseconds.

cards.title: Neuroplasticity
cards.text: The brain rewires itself throughout life. Learning a skill strengthens connections between neurons that fire together; unused ones weaken.

cards.title: Learning to juggle
cards.text: Studies found that adults who learnt to juggle for three months showed growth in brain areas that track moving objects, which shrank back when they stopped.

quiz.q: How many neurons does the human brain have, roughly?
What part of the brain coordinates balance?
Do we use only 10% of our brain?
options: No, we use virtually all of it

lessons.title: Food and digestion
lessons.summary: From your plate to your cells.

cards.title: The journey
cards.text: Food travels through about 9 metres of digestive tract, from mouth to exit, over roughly one to three days.

cards.title: Mouth and teeth
cards.text: Teeth grind food and saliva starts digesting starch. Chewing well means less work for the stomach.

cards.title: The stomach
cards.text: The stomach churns food with strong acid (pH around 1.5–3.5) and enzymes that break down protein. Mucus protects its own lining from being digested.

cards.title: Small intestine
cards.text: Most nutrients are absorbed in the small intestine. Its lining is covered with tiny finger-like villi, giving a huge surface area.

cards.title: Large intestine
cards.text: The large intestine absorbs water and salt and is home to trillions of gut bacteria that help digest fibre and make some vitamins.

cards.title: The microbiome
cards.text: Your gut holds about as many bacterial cells as you have human cells. A varied diet with fibre feeds a varied microbiome.

cards.title: Three macronutrients
cards.text: Food gives energy from carbohydrates, fats and proteins. Fat has more than twice the energy per gram.

cards.title: The liver
cards.text: The liver is the body's chemical factory: it processes nutrients, stores energy as glycogen, makes bile to digest fat and breaks down toxins and alcohol.

cards.title: Feeling full
cards.text: After eating, stretch sensors and hormones signal fullness, but it takes about 20 minutes to register. Eating slowly helps you notice it in time.

cards.title: Water
cards.text: Adults need roughly 1.5–2 litres of fluids a day from drinks, more in heat or exercise. About 20% of our water comes from food.

quiz.q: Where are most nutrients absorbed?
quiz.explain: Its villi give a huge surface.

quiz.q: Which nutrient has the most energy per gram?

cards.title: Lines of defence
cards.text: The body defends in layers: barriers keep germs out, the innate system attacks anything foreign quickly, and the adaptive system learns specific enemies.

cards.title: Barriers
cards.text: Skin, mucus, tears, stomach acid and coughing all stop most germs before they get inside.

cards.title: Inflammation
cards.text: When germs get in, the area becomes red, warm, swollen and sore. Blood vessels widen to bring in defending cells: it's a sign the immune system is working.

cards.title: White blood cells
cards.text: Several kinds of white blood cells share the work: some swallow invaders, some make antibodies, and some destroy infected cells.

cards.title: Antibodies
cards.text: Antibodies are Y-shaped proteins that lock onto one specific invader, like a key in a lock, marking it for destruction.

cards.title: Immune memory
cards.text: After an infection, memory cells stay for years. If the same germ returns, the body responds faster and stronger, often before you feel ill.

cards.title: Vaccines
cards.text: A vaccine shows the immune system a harmless piece or version of a germ, so it builds memory without having the disease. Edward Jenner made the first vaccine, against smallpox, in 1796.

cards.title: Herd immunity
cards.text: When enough people are immune, a germ can't spread easily, protecting those who can't be vaccinated, like newborns. Smallpox was eradicated worldwide in 1980.

cards.title: Bacteria vs viruses
cards.text: Bacteria are living cells that antibiotics can kill. Viruses are much smaller and hijack our cells to copy themselves; antibiotics don't work on them.

cards.title: Fever
cards.text: A fever is the body turning up its thermostat. Higher temperature slows many germs and speeds up immune cells.

quiz.q: What do vaccines train?
Do antibiotics work against viruses like the flu?

lessons.title: Senses and skeleton
lessons.summary: How you sense the world and hold yourself up.

cards.title: More than five senses
cards.text: Besides sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch, you sense balance, temperature, pain and the position of your limbs (proprioception), which lets you touch your nose with eyes closed.

cards.title: How eyes see
cards.text: Light enters through the cornea and lens, which focus an upside-down image on the retina. The brain flips it and builds the picture we see.

cards.title: Rods and cones
cards.text: The retina has rods for dim light and movement, and cones for colour. Three kinds of cones sense red, green and blue light.

cards.title: How ears hear
cards.text: Sound waves make the eardrum vibrate. Three tiny bones pass the vibration to the fluid-filled cochlea, where hair cells turn it into nerve signals.

cards.title: Taste is mostly smell
cards.text: The tongue detects five basic tastes; most "flavour" actually comes from smell. That's why food tastes bland with a blocked nose.

cards.title: The skeleton
cards.text: Adults have 206 bones; babies have about 300, which fuse as they grow. More than half of them are in the hands and feet.

cards.title: Bones are alive
cards.text: Bones are living tissue that constantly rebuild. They store calcium, and the marrow inside makes blood cells. Exercise and weight-bearing make bones stronger.

cards.title: Muscles
cards.text: There are about 600 muscles. Skeletal muscles can only pull, never push, so they work in pairs, like the biceps and triceps.

cards.title: Three types of muscle
cards.text: Skeletal muscles move bones by choice; smooth muscle moves food and blood vessels automatically; cardiac muscle in the heart never tires.

cards.title: Smallest and largest
cards.text: The smallest bone is the stirrup in the ear, about 3 mm. The largest is the thigh bone, the femur, roughly a quarter of your height.

quiz.q: How many bones does an adult have?
Why does food taste bland with a cold?
quiz.explain: The nose does most of the work.

lessons.title: Lungs and breathing
lessons.summary: How every breath keeps you alive.

cards.title: The airway
cards.text: Air goes in through the nose or mouth, down the windpipe (trachea), into two bronchi, then branches again and again into tiny tubes ending in air sacs.

cards.title: Alveoli
cards.text: The lungs hold about 480 million tiny air sacs called alveoli. Spread flat, their surface would cover roughly a badminton court.

cards.title: Gas exchange
cards.text: In the alveoli, oxygen passes into the blood and carbon dioxide passes out, simply by moving from where there's more to where there's less.

cards.title: The diaphragm
cards.text: Breathing is driven mainly by the diaphragm, a dome-shaped muscle under the lungs. It flattens to pull air in and relaxes to let it out.

cards.title: What triggers breathing
cards.text: Your urge to breathe comes mostly from rising carbon dioxide, not falling oxygen. Sensors in the brainstem measure it in the blood.

cards.title: Breaths by the numbers
cards.text: At rest, adults breathe about 12–20 times a minute, around 20,000 times a day. Each breath moves about half a litre of air.

cards.title: Air we breathe
cards.text: Air is about 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen. The air you breathe out still has about 16% oxygen, which is why rescue breaths work.

cards.title: Cleaning the air
cards.text: Hairs and sticky mucus trap dust and germs. Tiny beating hairs called cilia sweep the mucus up to the throat, where you swallow it.

cards.title: Altitude

viz.unit: oxygen per breath, % of sea level

cards.text: Higher up, each breath carries less oxygen. Above about 2,500 m some people get altitude sickness. Over weeks, the body makes more red blood cells to adapt.

cards.title: Slow breathing
cards.text: Breathing slowly, about six breaths a minute with longer exhales, activates the body's calming system and lowers heart rate within minutes.

quiz.q: What triggers the urge to breathe?
Which muscle drives breathing?
Roughly what percentage of air is oxygen?

cards.title: How many cells?

items.l: bacteria living on and in you

cards.text: An adult body has about 30–37 trillion human cells of more than 200 types, from nerve cells a metre long to tiny red blood cells.

cards.title: Inside a cell
cards.text: A cell is like a factory: the nucleus holds the instructions, mitochondria make energy, ribosomes build proteins and the membrane controls what goes in and out.

cards.title: Mitochondria
cards.text: Mitochondria turn food and oxygen into ATP, the cell's energy currency. They have their own DNA, inherited only from your mother.

cards.title: DNA in every cell
cards.text: Each cell holds about 2 metres of DNA, coiled into 46 chromosomes in a nucleus far smaller than a pinhead.

cards.title: From gene to protein
cards.text: A gene is copied into messenger RNA, which travels to a ribosome. The ribosome reads it three letters at a time and builds a protein.

cards.title: Cell division
cards.text: Cells copy themselves by mitosis: the DNA duplicates, the chromosomes separate and the cell splits into two identical cells.

cards.title: Cells renew at different rates
cards.text: Some cells are replaced constantly, others last a lifetime. Most of the neurons in your brain's cortex are as old as you are.

cards.title: Stem cells
cards.text: Stem cells can turn into many other cell types. They repair tissues and are used in treatments like bone-marrow transplants.

cards.title: When cells go wrong
cards.text: Cancer begins when mutations make a cell ignore the signals that control division. It multiplies out of control and may spread.

cards.title: Seeing cells
cards.text: Robert Hooke named "cells" in 1665 after the little rooms he saw in cork. Van Leeuwenhoek first saw living bacteria and sperm cells in the 1670s.

quiz.q: What do mitochondria do?
How much DNA is in a single cell?

lessons.title: Sleep
lessons.summary: Why we spend a third of life asleep.

cards.title: How much sleep?
cards.text: Most adults need 7–9 hours a night; teenagers need 8–10; young children even more. Few people truly thrive on less than 6.

cards.title: Sleep cycles
cards.text: Sleep runs in cycles of about 90 minutes, moving from light sleep to deep sleep and then to REM sleep, when most vivid dreams happen. We go through 4–6 cycles a night.

cards.title: Deep sleep
cards.text: In deep sleep, the body repairs tissues, releases growth hormone and the brain's waste-clearing system washes away by-products of the day.

cards.title: REM sleep
cards.text: During REM, the eyes dart around, the brain is very active and the body's muscles are temporarily paralysed so we don't act out our dreams.

cards.title: The body clock
cards.text: A master clock in the brain keeps a roughly 24-hour circadian rhythm, reset each day mainly by morning light.

cards.title: Melatonin
cards.text: As darkness falls, the brain releases melatonin, the "darkness hormone". Bright screens late at night can delay it.

cards.title: Caffeine

viz.unit: caffeine left, mg (from 100 mg at 3 pm)

cards.text: Caffeine blocks adenosine, the chemical that builds sleep pressure during the day. Its half-life is about 5 hours, so an afternoon coffee can still affect sleep at night.

cards.title: Sleep debt
cards.text: Too little sleep hurts attention, mood, memory and immunity. Being awake for 24 hours impairs driving about as much as being over the legal alcohol limit.

cards.title: Larks and owls
cards.text: People differ in their natural timing, called chronotype. Larks wake early easily; owls peak later. Teenagers shift later for biological reasons.

cards.title: Better sleep habits
cards.text: Consistent times, morning daylight, a cool dark room, no caffeine after lunch and screens away an hour before bed help most people sleep better.

quiz.q: How long is a typical sleep cycle?
What does caffeine block?

cards.title: The largest organ
cards.text: Skin is the body's largest organ: about 2 m² and several kilograms in an adult. It protects, senses, controls temperature and makes vitamin D.

cards.title: Three layers
cards.text: The epidermis is the protective outer layer, the dermis holds nerves, blood vessels, sweat glands and hair roots, and the fatty layer beneath insulates and cushions.

cards.title: Skin renews

steps: New cells form at the base

cards.text: You shed tens of thousands of dead skin cells every minute. The outer layer replaces itself roughly every month; much household dust contains skin flakes.

cards.title: Sweat
cards.text: Sweat cools you as it evaporates. Humans have 2–4 million sweat glands, one reason we're among the best long-distance runners in the animal world.

cards.title: Skin colour
cards.text: Skin colour comes from melanin, which absorbs UV light. Human populations evolved different amounts depending on sunlight where their ancestors lived.

cards.title: Sun protection
cards.text: UV radiation damages skin DNA, causing sunburn, ageing and skin cancer. Shade, clothing and sunscreen with SPF 30 or more help, especially at midday.

cards.title: Hair
cards.text: You have about 5 million hair follicles, and around 100,000 on your scalp. Each hair grows about 1 cm a month, then rests and falls out.

cards.title: Goosebumps
cards.text: Goosebumps are tiny muscles pulling hairs upright. In furry ancestors it trapped warm air or made them look bigger; in us it's mostly a leftover.

cards.title: Nails
cards.text: Nails are made of keratin, like hair. Fingernails grow about 3 mm a month, faster than toenails, and faster in summer.

cards.title: Healing a cut
cards.text: A cut heals in stages: bleeding stops with a clot, white cells clean the wound, new tissue fills it and a scar slowly remodels over months.

quiz.q: What gives skin its colour?
About how fast does hair grow?
quiz.explain: Then it rests and falls out.

cards.title: Chemical messages
cards.text: Hormones are messengers released into the blood by glands. They travel everywhere but only act on cells with the right receptors, like a key fitting a lock.

cards.title: Nerves vs hormones
cards.text: Nerves send fast, precise signals; hormones send slower, longer-lasting, widespread signals.

cards.title: The glands
cards.text: Key glands include the pituitary (the "master gland"), thyroid, adrenals, pancreas and the ovaries or testes.

cards.title: Insulin
cards.text: After a meal, the pancreas releases insulin, which lets cells take up sugar from the blood. Glucagon does the opposite when sugar runs low.

cards.title: Adrenaline
cards.text: In a fright, the adrenal glands release adrenaline within seconds: faster heart, wider airways, more sugar in the blood. Ready to act.

cards.title: Cortisol
cards.text: Cortisol is released during longer stress and follows a daily rhythm, peaking soon after waking. Chronically high levels can affect sleep and immunity.

cards.title: Thyroid
cards.text: The thyroid in your neck sets your metabolic rate, how fast your body uses energy. It needs iodine, which is why table salt is often iodised.

cards.title: Growth hormone
cards.text: Growth hormone from the pituitary drives growth in childhood and is mostly released during deep sleep. It also helps repair tissues in adults.

cards.title: Hunger hormones
cards.text: Ghrelin rises before meals and makes you hungry; leptin, from fat tissue, signals you have enough stored energy.

cards.title: Feedback loops
cards.text: Most hormones work like a thermostat: when a level rises too high, a signal shuts down production, keeping things balanced.

quiz.q: Which hormone lowers blood sugar?
Why is table salt often iodised?

cards.title: Two filters
cards.text: You have two fist-sized kidneys at the back of your abdomen. Together they filter about 180 litres of blood plasma a day and return almost all of it.

cards.title: Nephrons
cards.text: Each kidney contains about a million tiny filtering units called nephrons. They let water and small molecules through, then reabsorb what the body needs.

cards.title: What kidneys remove
cards.text: Kidneys remove urea (from protein breakdown), extra salt, excess water and many medicines, keeping blood chemistry within tight limits.

cards.title: Water balance
cards.text: When you're short of water, the brain releases a hormone that makes kidneys save it, so urine gets darker. Drink plenty and urine is pale.

cards.title: Urine colour guide
cards.text: Pale straw colour usually means you're well hydrated; dark amber suggests you need to drink. Some foods and vitamins change colour too.

cards.title: Blood pressure control
cards.text: Kidneys help control blood pressure by adjusting how much salt and water the body keeps, and by releasing hormones that tighten blood vessels.

cards.title: More jobs
cards.text: Kidneys also make a hormone that tells bone marrow to make red blood cells, and activate vitamin D for strong bones.

cards.title: Kidney stones
cards.text: Minerals in urine can crystallise into stones, which can be very painful when they move. Drinking enough water is the main prevention.

cards.title: Living with one kidney
cards.text: One healthy kidney can do the work of two, which is why living kidney donation is possible. The first successful kidney transplant was in 1954.

cards.title: The bladder
cards.text: The bladder stores urine, holding about 400–600 ml. Stretch sensors signal the urge to go well before it's full.

quiz.q: How much blood plasma do the kidneys filter daily?
Dark urine usually suggests…
Can people live with one kidney?
options: Yes, one healthy kidney is enough

lessons.title: Muscles and exercise
lessons.summary: How movement works and why it matters.

cards.title: How muscles contract
cards.text: Muscle fibres contain filaments that slide past each other, pulled by tiny molecular "oars". Billions of them shortening together make a muscle contract.

cards.title: Fast and slow fibres
cards.text: Slow-twitch fibres resist fatigue and suit endurance; fast-twitch fibres are powerful but tire quickly. Marathon runners and sprinters have different mixes.

cards.title: Energy systems
cards.text: For a few seconds, muscles use stored fuel; for about a minute, they burn sugar without oxygen, making lactate; beyond that, they rely on oxygen.

cards.title: Why muscles grow
cards.text: Strength training creates small damage and stress in fibres. During recovery, the body rebuilds them thicker and stronger, if you eat enough protein and rest.

cards.title: Use it or lose it
cards.text: Without use, muscles shrink quickly; a week in bed can cost noticeable strength. From around 30–40, muscle mass declines slowly unless you train.

cards.title: Cardio benefits
cards.text: Aerobic exercise strengthens the heart, lowers blood pressure and resting heart rate, and improves mood and sleep.

cards.title: Activity guidelines
cards.text: The WHO recommends adults get 150–300 minutes of moderate activity a week, plus muscle-strengthening at least twice a week.

cards.title: Stretching and warm-up
cards.text: A warm-up raises muscle temperature and readies joints. Dynamic movements before exercise work better than long static stretches.

cards.title: Soreness

items.r: Small fibre damage and repair do

cards.text: Muscle soreness a day or two after unusual exercise is normal and comes from small fibre damage, not "lactic acid build-up".

cards.title: Small steps count
cards.text: Even short bursts help. Taking the stairs, walking during calls and a 10-minute walk after meals add up and improve blood sugar.

quiz.q: What causes next-day muscle soreness?
How much moderate activity does the WHO recommend weekly?
quiz.explain: Plus strength training twice a week.

lessons.title: Growing and ageing
lessons.summary: From a single cell to old age.

cards.title: One cell to trillions
cards.text: You began as a single fertilised egg. By birth, after about 40 weeks, you had trillions of cells organised into organs.

cards.title: Newborn surprises
cards.text: Newborns have about 300 bones, can't see far and can recognise their mother's voice, heard in the womb.

cards.title: Baby brains
cards.text: A baby's brain doubles in size in the first year. Billions of connections form; unused ones are later pruned.

cards.title: Puberty
cards.text: Hormones from the brain trigger puberty, usually between about 8 and 14. Growth spurts, voice changes and brain reorganisation follow.

cards.title: The teenage brain
cards.text: The prefrontal cortex, which handles planning and self-control, keeps maturing until the mid-20s, while reward systems mature earlier.

cards.title: Peak years
cards.text: Different abilities peak at different ages. Speed and muscle often peak in the 20s; vocabulary and knowledge keep growing into the 60s and beyond.

cards.title: Why we age
cards.text: Ageing comes from accumulated damage: DNA errors, worn proteins, shrinking chromosome tips called telomeres and cells that stop dividing.

cards.title: Life expectancy
cards.text: Life expectancy at birth in Portugal rose from about 63 in 1960 to over 81 today, thanks to vaccines, clean water, nutrition and healthcare.

cards.title: Blue zones
cards.text: Regions where people often live past 100, like Okinawa and Sardinia, share habits: daily movement, plant-rich diets, strong social ties and purpose.

cards.title: Ageing well
cards.text: Evidence points to a few big levers: stay active, keep muscles strong, sleep well, don't smoke, keep learning and stay connected with people.

quiz.q: When does the brain's planning region finish maturing?
How many bones does a newborn have?

lessons.title: Genes and heredity
lessons.summary: Why you look like your family.

cards.title: Half from each parent
cards.text: You inherit 23 chromosomes from your mother and 23 from your father. Each pair carries two versions of most genes.

cards.title: Mendel's peas
cards.text: In the 1860s, monk Gregor Mendel bred pea plants and found traits pass in predictable ratios. He's the father of genetics, though ignored until 1900.

cards.title: Dominant and recessive
cards.text: A dominant version shows up if you have one copy; a recessive one only shows if you have two. Two brown-eyed parents can have a blue-eyed child.

cards.title: Boy or girl
cards.text: Usually, two X chromosomes lead to female development and an X with a Y to male. The father's sperm carries either an X or a Y.

cards.title: Most traits are complex
cards.text: Height, intelligence and most diseases are shaped by hundreds of genes plus environment. There's no single "height gene".

cards.title: Nature and nurture
cards.text: Twin studies compare identical and non-identical twins to estimate how much variation comes from genes. For most traits, both matter a lot.

cards.title: The Human Genome Project
cards.text: Completed in 2003, it read the 3 billion letters of human DNA. The first genome cost about $3 billion; today one costs a few hundred dollars.

cards.title: We're 99.9% the same
cards.text: Any two people share about 99.9% of their DNA. Humans also share about 98–99% with chimpanzees and around 60% of genes with bananas.

cards.title: Epigenetics
cards.text: Chemical tags on DNA switch genes on and off without changing the code. Diet, stress and environment can change these tags.

cards.title: Gene editing
cards.text: CRISPR, developed in 2012, lets scientists cut and edit DNA precisely. In 2023 the first CRISPR-based treatment was approved, for sickle cell disease.

quiz.q: Two brown-eyed parents can have a blue-eyed child because…
options: both carry a recessive blue version
quiz.explain: A 1 in 4 chance if both are Bb.

quiz.q: Who discovered the basic rules of inheritance?

cards.title: Two sets
cards.text: Children have 20 baby teeth; adults have up to 32 permanent ones, including four wisdom teeth that often appear late, or never.

cards.title: Layers of a tooth
cards.text: Enamel, the hardest substance in the body, covers the crown. Beneath is dentine, and in the centre the pulp with nerves and blood vessels.

cards.title: How cavities form
cards.text: Bacteria in plaque eat sugars and make acid. Acid dissolves enamel; repeated attacks create a hole, a cavity.

cards.title: How often, not how much
cards.text: Each sugary snack starts a 20–30 minute acid attack. Sipping sweet drinks all day is worse for teeth than having the same sugar at once.

cards.title: Fluoride
cards.text: Fluoride makes enamel more resistant to acid and helps repair early damage. Brushing twice daily with fluoride toothpaste is the main protection.

cards.title: Brushing well
cards.text: Brush for two minutes, twice a day, then spit but don't rinse, so fluoride stays on teeth. Floss or interdental brushes clean between teeth.

cards.title: Gums matter
cards.text: Gum disease starts with bleeding gums and can lead to tooth loss. It's linked to heart disease and diabetes too.

cards.title: Saliva
cards.text: You make about 0.5–1.5 litres of saliva a day. It washes teeth, neutralises acid, starts digestion and helps you taste.

cards.title: Tooth types
cards.text: Incisors cut, canines tear, premolars and molars crush. Our mix of teeth reflects an omnivore's diet.

cards.title: Teeth tell stories
cards.text: Teeth record your life: archaeologists read diet, age and even where someone grew up from chemicals in tooth enamel.

quiz.q: What is the hardest substance in the body?
After brushing, you should…

cards.title: Hippocrates
cards.text: Around 400 BCE, Hippocrates taught that diseases have natural causes, not divine ones, and that doctors should observe carefully. The Hippocratic Oath is named after him.

cards.title: Four humours
cards.text: For 2,000 years, doctors believed health depended on balancing four fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile. It led to bloodletting, which often did harm.

cards.title: Anatomy
cards.text: In 1543 Andreas Vesalius published accurate drawings of the human body from dissections, correcting many errors that had been believed since ancient times.

cards.title: Circulation
cards.text: In 1628 William Harvey showed that the heart pumps blood around the body in a closed loop, rather than the liver constantly making new blood.

cards.title: Germ theory
cards.text: In the 1860s, Louis Pasteur and Robert Koch showed that microbes cause many diseases. It transformed medicine, food safety and hygiene.

cards.title: Washing hands
cards.text: In 1847 Ignaz Semmelweis cut deaths of new mothers dramatically by making doctors wash their hands. Colleagues mocked him; he was proved right after his death.

cards.title: Anaesthesia
cards.text: Surgery before 1846 meant enduring pain fully awake. Ether, and then chloroform, made long, careful operations possible.

cards.title: Penicillin
cards.text: In 1928 Alexander Fleming noticed mould killing bacteria on a plate. Developed into a drug in the 1940s, penicillin and later antibiotics saved hundreds of millions of lives.

cards.title: A Portuguese Nobel
cards.text: Egas Moniz won Portugal's first Nobel Prize, in 1949, for the lobotomy, now abandoned and controversial. His invention of cerebral angiography, imaging brain blood vessels, has lasted.

cards.title: Modern medicine
cards.text: Recent decades brought imaging scans, organ transplants, keyhole surgery, mRNA vaccines and targeted cancer drugs.

quiz.q: Who showed that handwashing saves lives?
Who discovered penicillin?
What did Harvey show in 1628?
quiz.explain: The heart pumps blood around the body.

cards.title: What vitamins are
cards.text: Vitamins are compounds the body needs in tiny amounts but mostly can't make. There are 13, divided into fat-soluble and water-soluble.

cards.title: Scurvy and vitamin C
cards.text: Sailors on long voyages got scurvy: bleeding gums and weakness. In 1747 James Lind showed citrus fruit cured it. Vasco da Gama's crew suffered terribly from it.

cards.title: Vitamin D
cards.text: Your skin makes vitamin D in sunlight. It helps absorb calcium for bones. In winter at northern latitudes, many people run low.

cards.title: Vitamin A
cards.text: Vitamin A is vital for vision in dim light and for immunity. Carrots, sweet potatoes and leafy greens provide it as beta-carotene.

cards.title: B12
cards.text: Vitamin B12 is found almost only in animal foods, so people on vegan diets usually need fortified foods or supplements.

cards.title: Iron
cards.text: Iron carries oxygen in haemoglobin. Vitamin C helps absorb iron from plants; tea and coffee with meals reduce it.

cards.title: Calcium
cards.text: About 99% of the body's calcium is in bones and teeth. Dairy, canned fish with bones, tofu and greens are good sources.

cards.title: Salt
cards.text: We need some sodium, but most people eat far more than the WHO limit of 5 g of salt a day. Much of it hides in bread, processed meats and ready meals.

cards.title: Fibre
cards.text: Fibre feeds gut bacteria, keeps digestion regular and helps control blood sugar and cholesterol. Most adults eat too little; aim for about 25–30 g a day.

cards.title: Food first

items.r: Varied food first, supplements for specific needs

cards.text: For most healthy people, a varied diet supplies what they need. Supplements help in specific cases, like vitamin D in winter or folic acid in pregnancy; more isn't better.

quiz.q: Which vitamin did sailors lack when they got scurvy?
What reduces iron absorption from a meal?

lessons.title: Stress and the body
lessons.summary: Why stress helps, and when it harms.

cards.title: The stress response
cards.text: Stress triggers two systems: a fast nerve response with adrenaline, and a slower hormone response with cortisol, preparing body and mind for a challenge.

cards.title: Good stress
cards.text: Short bursts of stress sharpen focus and performance: think of an exam or a race. The problem is stress that never switches off.

cards.title: The performance curve
cards.text: Performance rises with arousal up to a point, then falls. Too little stress is boring; too much overwhelms. Psychologists call it the Yerkes–Dodson law.

cards.title: Stress and the heart
cards.text: Long-term stress raises blood pressure and heart-disease risk. Sudden extreme stress can even cause temporary "broken heart syndrome".

cards.title: Stress and the gut
cards.text: The gut and brain talk constantly. Stress can cause stomach aches, nausea or bowel changes; "butterflies in the stomach" are real.

cards.title: Stress and immunity
cards.text: Brief stress mobilises immune cells; chronic stress suppresses immunity. Students catch more colds during exam season.

cards.title: Rest and digest
cards.text: The parasympathetic system is the counterweight to fight-or-flight: it slows the heart and restarts digestion. Slow breathing switches it on.

cards.title: What helps
cards.text: Evidence-based stress relievers include exercise, sleep, time in nature, talking to friends, slow breathing and limiting news and alcohol.

cards.title: Reappraisal

items.r: "My body is getting ready to perform"

cards.text: Seeing a pounding heart as "my body getting ready" rather than "I'm panicking" improves performance in studies. How you interpret stress matters.

cards.title: Box breathing
cards.text: Used by pilots and athletes: breathe in for 4, hold for 4, out for 4, hold for 4. Repeat four times.

quiz.q: What does the Yerkes–Dodson law say?
options: Moderate arousal gives the best performance
quiz.explain: Too little or too much hurts performance.

quiz.q: Which system slows the heart and restarts digestion?

cards.title: Pain is a protector
cards.text: Pain warns of damage. People born unable to feel pain often injure themselves badly without noticing.

cards.title: Nociceptors
cards.text: Special nerve endings called nociceptors detect harmful heat, pressure or chemicals and send signals to the spinal cord and brain.

cards.title: Fast and slow pain
cards.text: Stub a toe and you feel a sharp, quick pain first, then a dull ache. They travel along different nerve fibres at different speeds.

cards.title: The brain decides
cards.text: Pain is made by the brain, not the injury alone. Attention, fear and context can turn it up or down. Soldiers have ignored serious wounds in battle.

cards.title: The gate theory
cards.text: Rubbing a bumped elbow helps because touch signals compete with pain signals at "gates" in the spinal cord.

cards.title: Referred pain
cards.text: Pain can be felt far from its source. Heart problems can show up as arm or jaw pain because nerves share pathways.

cards.title: Phantom limbs
cards.text: Many amputees feel the missing limb, sometimes painfully. Mirror therapy, which tricks the brain with a reflection, can help.

cards.title: Painkillers
cards.text: Paracetamol and anti-inflammatories like ibuprofen work differently. Anti-inflammatories block chemicals that sensitise nerves; opioids act on the brain and spinal cord.

cards.title: Placebo
cards.text: A sugar pill can reduce pain when people expect it to, because expectation triggers the brain's own pain-relief chemicals. Placebos work best for pain and nausea.

cards.title: Chronic pain
cards.text: When pain lasts beyond three months, the nervous system itself can become oversensitive. Treatment often combines movement, therapy and medicine.

quiz.q: Why does rubbing a bumped elbow help?
options: Touch signals compete with pain signals

quiz.q: Why can heart problems cause arm pain?

cards.title: Why we yawn

items: Even dogs catch it from us

cards.text: Yawning may cool the brain and increase alertness. It's contagious: seeing, hearing or even reading about yawning can make you yawn.

cards.title: Hiccups
cards.text: Hiccups are sudden spasms of the diaphragm, with the vocal cords snapping shut to make the "hic". Charles Osborne hiccuped for 68 years.

cards.title: Your stomach lining
cards.text: Stomach acid is strong enough to dissolve some metals, so the stomach renews its protective lining every few days.

cards.title: Fingerprints
cards.text: Fingerprints form before birth and are unique, even between identical twins. They may improve grip and touch sensitivity.

cards.title: Funny bone
cards.text: Hitting your "funny bone" actually hits the ulnar nerve, which runs close to the skin at the elbow. That's why it tingles down to your little finger.

cards.title: Taller in the morning
cards.text: You're about 1 cm taller in the morning: the discs in your spine compress during the day and recover overnight.

cards.title: Stomach rumbles
cards.text: Borborygmi, stomach rumbles, are gas and fluid moving through the gut. They're loudest when empty because there's less food to muffle them.

cards.title: Brain freeze
cards.text: Cold food on the roof of your mouth makes blood vessels constrict and then quickly widen, causing a sharp headache for a few seconds.

cards.title: Belly button
cards.text: Your navel is a scar from the umbilical cord. Belly buttons host hundreds of species of bacteria.

cards.title: Goosebumps from music
cards.text: About half of people get "frisson", chills from moving music. It's linked to dopamine release at emotional peaks.

quiz.q: What is the "funny bone"?
quiz.explain: It runs close to the skin.

quiz.q: Why are you taller in the morning?
